title: Many forms of penance (CCC 1434–1439)
hookLine: fasting, prayer, almsgiving, reconciliation, care for the poor

lines: A ROSARY, FASTING, COINS, A PHONE CALL.
cards: A rosary prayed on a long bus ride. A skipped lunch on a Friday. Coins dropped into a box by the church door.
A phone call to a brother after a long silence. A quiet hour at a soup kitchen. Lined up like that, they look like five different hobbies.
The Catechism puts acts like these on one list. The turning of the heart doesn't stay inside, it says. It comes out through the hands, the mouth, the wallet, the calendar, and in more than one shape.

teach.b: Back on day one hundred thirty-six, penance was the small task given after absolution, to begin the repair. The Catechism's list is far wider.

It starts with three: Scripture and the Fathers, it says, insist above all on fasting, prayer and almsgiving. They come from the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus says to give, pray and fast in secret, without an audience.
One old way to read them: fasting turns you toward yourself, prayer toward God, almsgiving toward your neighbor. Three directions, one turn.
Then the list keeps going: making peace, tears of sorrow, concern for a neighbor's salvation, asking the saints to pray, and above all charity.

teach.h: CHARITY COVERETH A MULTITUDE OF SINS.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "charity covereth a multitude of sins." Then it gets almost ordinary.

teach.h: IN DAILY LIFE, NOT ONCE A YEAR.
teach.b: Conversion happens in daily life, it says: reconciliation, concern for the poor, standing up for what is just, owning your faults, honest correction between friends, looking over your life, examining your conscience, accepting suffering.
It quotes Jesus in Luke: "let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." Daily, not once a year.
The Church gives the year a rhythm for it: Lent, and each Friday, as days of penance. Reading Scripture counts. The Our Father counts.
The Eucharist itself, the Catechism says, feeds this turning. A teenager who apologizes first. A retiree reading the Gospel each morning.
Someone who gives up scrolling to sit with a lonely neighbor. All on the list. And the Catechism ends with the prodigal son, who turns toward home and finds his father already running down the road.

how: Catholics keep penance through fasting and abstinence in Lent and on Fridays, through prayer and giving to the poor, and through everyday acts of reconciliation and charity, alongside the sacrament of confession.

games.q: what does “many forms of penance” mean?
o: fasting, prayer, giving and everyday turns back
harsh acts of self-punishment for past sins
only the prayers a priest gives after confession

games.q: the forms of penance — tap the pairs.

s: penance only means the sacrament of confession
the Catechism lists many forms: fasting, prayer, almsgiving, reconciliation, care for the poor, charity.
the Catechism names fasting, prayer and almsgiving above all
it says Scripture and the Fathers insist on those three.
Lent is the only time of penance in the Church's year
each Friday is set aside as a day of penance too.

games.q: you want to turn back toward God and your neighbor, and the word penance sounds heavy. where does the Catechism say it happens?
o: only in a church, once a year.
in daily life: reconciliation, care for the poor, honesty.
games.why: the Catechism says conversion happens in daily life, and quotes Jesus: "take up his cross daily."

practice: Let the list pass slowly: fasting from something small, a prayer, a gift to someone in need, a message that makes peace, an honest look at a fault.

Don't pick the most impressive one; notice the one that tugs at you, a little uncomfortable in a useful way, and picture when you could do it. If you pray, offer that small turn to God; if you don't, just keep it in view.

wordCard.voice: Many forms of penance. Fasting, prayer and almsgiving first, and then a long list of everyday turns: reconciliation, care for the poor, honesty, charity. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: many ways back. None of them has to be big. See you tomorrow.
